title: Swiss Maestro
clues: His balletic all-court game defined elegance and efficiency for much of the 2000s.
First man to reach 20 Grand Slam singles titles, spanning all four majors.
Claimed a record eight Wimbledon singles crowns, ruling the grass at SW19.
Held ATP No. 1 for a record 237 consecutive weeks, within 310 total weeks atop the rankings.
In 2017, returned from a six-month layoff to win the Australian Open, then added an eighth Wimbledon at age 35.

title: American 'Queen of the Court' Powerhouse
clues: American legend who dominated across two decades and spent 319 weeks as world No. 1.
Her booming serve is widely regarded as the world's best in women's tennis.
Holds the Open Era record with 23 Grand Slam singles titles.
Twice held all four major singles titles at once (2002–03 and 2014–15).
Won the 2017 Australian Open while roughly eight weeks pregnant and is the younger half of a famed sister duo.

title: American ‘Pistol Pete’ Powerhouse
clues: Ruled men’s tennis through much of the 1990s with a majestic serve-and-volley game.
Ended six straight seasons as year-end world No. 1 from 1993 to 1998.
Captured 14 Grand Slam singles titles, including a record seven at Wimbledon.
Celebrated for having the world’s best second serve, especially in tiebreaks and clutch moments.
Closed his career by winning the 2002 US Open final over Andre Agassi in his last professional match.

title: Serbian Return Machine
clues: Has held the ATP world No. 1 ranking for the most weeks in history.
Renowned for the world's best return of serve and near-impenetrable baseline defense.
Captured three majors in a single season multiple times, including 2011, 2015, 2021, and 2023.
Completed the Career Grand Slam and became the first man to win each major at least three times.
Serbian star nicknamed 'Nole' and 'The Djoker,' holder of a men's-record 24 Grand Slam singles titles.

title: American 'Ice Maiden' of Baseline Mastery
clues: American star who dominated women’s tennis through the 1970s and 1980s with icy composure from the baseline.
Reached a record 34 Grand Slam singles finals and won 18 major singles titles.
The first official WTA world No. 1 in 1975; totaled 260 weeks at No. 1.
Owns the best clay-court winning percentage in the Open Era and a 125-match win streak on clay, including a record 7 French Open singles titles.
Her era-defining rivalry with Martina Navratilova and the cool nickname she earned point straight to her identity.

title: Belgian “Juju” with the Golden One‑Handed Backhand
clues: Former WTA world No. 1 who finished three seasons as year‑end No. 1 in the 2000s.
Winner of seven major singles titles, with clay as her most dominant surface.
Olympic singles gold medalist at Athens 2004.
Completed a Roland Garros three‑peat from 2005–2007 and added the 2007 US Open title.
Her elegant one‑handed backhand is widely hailed as the world’s best in the women’s game.

title: Australian 'Rusty' With Relentless Fight
clues: Australian former world No. 1 famed for relentless counterpunching and shouted “C’mon!” celebrations.
Became the youngest year-end ATP No. 1 in history at age 20.
Finished both 2001 and 2002 as the ATP year-end No. 1.
Won the 2001 US Open final in straight sets over Pete Sampras.
Added a Wimbledon singles title in 2002 and is widely known by the nickname “Rusty.”

title: German “Fraulein Forehand” Phenomenon
clues: A former world No. 1 who dominated women’s tennis across all surfaces from the late 1980s into the 1990s.
She spent a record 377 total weeks atop the WTA rankings.
Her explosive forehand—earning her the moniker “Fraulein Forehand”—was widely regarded as the world’s best of her era.
She captured 22 Grand Slam singles titles, completing the Career Grand Slam.
In 1988, she achieved the only calendar-year Golden Slam in singles: all four majors plus Olympic gold.

title: Czech-American “Queen of Grass”
clues: Czech-born, later naturalized American, she dominated both singles and doubles with supreme athleticism and net play.
Held the world No. 1 ranking in both singles and doubles for extended stretches in the 1980s.
Owns a record nine Wimbledon singles titles in the Open Era.
At her peak she produced an 86–1 season and a 74‑match winning streak that defined early‑1980s women’s tennis.
Her rivalry with Chris Evert spanned 80 matches (she led it), and at age 49 she won the US Open mixed doubles, finishing with 59 major titles across all disciplines.

title: British 'Muzza' Comeback King
clues: Former ATP world No. 1 and multiple Grand Slam singles champion of the 2010s.
A counterpunching baseliner famed for tireless defense and tactical guile.
Ended a 77-year wait for his country by winning the Wimbledon singles crown.
The only man to win back-to-back Olympic singles gold medals (2012, 2016).
Finished 2016 as year-end No. 1 after a 24-match win streak, then returned from hip resurfacing to win Antwerp in 2019.

title: Brazil’s “Guga” and the Heart on Clay
clues: A South American crowd favorite who rose to fame on red clay.
Captured three singles majors, all at Roland Garros.
Ended the 2000 season as world No. 1, the first South American to finish year-end No. 1 in the ATP era.
Famously drew a heart in the clay during his triumphant 2001 Paris run after surviving a nerve-jangling escape en route to the title.
Secured year-end No. 1 by toppling Sampras (semifinal) and Agassi (final) at the 2000 season-ending championships in Lisbon.

title: Russian “Octopus” of Hard Courts
clues: Former world No. 1 renowned for relentless success on hard courts and multiple Masters 1000 titles.
His elastic reach and flat strokes made him widely regarded as the world’s best at turning defense into offense on hard courts.
Became the first man outside the Big Four to claim ATP No. 1 in 18 years, achieving it in 2022.
Ended Novak Djokovic’s bid for a Calendar Grand Slam by winning the 2021 US Open final in straight sets.
Marked that New York breakthrough with a viral “dead fish” celebration, echoing his quirky on-court persona.

title: Australian “Barty Party” Maestro
clues: Australian former world No. 1 celebrated for all-court variety and calm under pressure.
She paused her tennis career to play professional cricket before returning to dominate the tour.
Her skidding backhand slice is widely hailed as the world's best, carving up grass and hard courts alike.
Captured majors on three surfaces: Roland Garros 2019, Wimbledon 2021, and the Australian Open 2022.
Ended a 44-year home-nation wait by winning AO 2022, then shocked the sport by retiring at age 25.

title: American 'The Punisher' Power Baseliner
clues: American former world No. 1 who captured eight Grand Slam singles titles across the 1990s and early 2000s.
Renowned for possessing the world's best return of serve, taking the ball extraordinarily early to rob opponents of time.
Completed the career Grand Slam at Roland Garros in 1999 after rallying from two sets down in the final.
Became the first man to achieve a Career Golden Slam in singles—adding 1996 Olympic gold in Atlanta to victories at all four majors.
Las Vegas-born champion who later married a 22-time Grand Slam winner from Germany.

title: Belgian 'Aussie Kim' Comeback Champion
clues: Former world No. 1 in singles and doubles from Belgium.
Won four Grand Slam singles titles, including three at the US Open.
Captured the 2009 US Open as an unseeded wild card just weeks into a comeback, becoming the first mother to win a major since 1980.
Widely known as “Aussie Kim,” she added the 2011 Australian Open to her résumé.
Teamed with Ai Sugiyama to win the 2003 French Open and Wimbledon doubles titles, and claimed the season-ending WTA Championships in 2002, 2003, and 2010.

title: German 'Boom Boom' Powerhouse
clues: Reached world No. 1 and finished his career with six major singles titles.
Explosive serve-and-volleyer who won three Wimbledon crowns and an Olympic doubles gold in 1992.
The first unseeded player and the first German man to capture the Wimbledon singles title.
Secured back-to-back Wimbledon triumphs as a teenager in 1985 and 1986, the first at just 17.
His thunderous serve earned him the enduring nickname “Boom Boom.”

title: Spanish "El Mosquito" with Whip-Forehand
clues: Spanish baseliner who ascended to world No. 1 in 2003.
Won Roland Garros in 2003 and reached the US Open final the same year.
Played a pivotal role in Spain’s first-ever Davis Cup title in 2000 with standout singles victories.
His fleet-footed style earned him a buzzing nickname that matched his speed and persistence.
Trademark weapon: in the early 2000s he was lauded for having the world's best clay-court forehand, a heavy, accurate whip that dictated rallies.

title: Belarusian “Vika” Baseline Enforcer
clues: Former WTA world No. 1 who became her country’s first-ever singles No. 1.
Captured back-to-back Australian Open singles crowns in 2012 and 2013.
Pulled off the Sunshine Double in 2016, winning Indian Wells and Miami in the same season.
Earned mixed doubles gold with Max Mirnyi and singles bronze at the London 2012 Olympics.
Known widely as “Vika,” she reached the US Open finals in 2012, 2013, and 2020.

title: German "Angie" with Iron-Wall Defense
clues: Left-handed German baseliner famed for tireless defense and counterpunching grit.
Rose to World No. 1 in 2016, finishing that season at the top of the WTA rankings.
Won two majors in 2016, including a breakthrough Australian Open final upset of Serena Williams.
Secured a third major at Wimbledon 2018 by defeating Serena Williams on Centre Court.
Claimed Olympic silver at Rio 2016 and captured the 2016 US Open by defeating Karolína Plíšková.

title: Swedish Gentleman of Serve-and-Volley
clues: A paragon of fair play whose classic serve-and-volley style defined late-80s and early-90s tennis.
Rose to world No. 1 and finished year-end No. 1 in both 1990 and 1991.
Won six major singles titles: two Australian Opens, two Wimbledons, and two US Opens.
Captured back-to-back US Open crowns in 1991 and 1992, defeating Jim Courier and then Pete Sampras in the finals.
Celebrated for possessing the world's best volleying touch of his era, with sublime first- and half-volleys at the net.
